overview: Middle English is the language of England between roughly 1150 and 1500 — the period that begins after the Norman Conquest had reshaped English vocabulary and ends as Caxton's printing press began standardizing it. Inflection collapsed dramatically from the four-case Old English system; word order grew fixed; thousands of French and Latin loans entered the lexicon; the Great Vowel Shift began in the late fourteenth century. The literary high point is the late fourteenth century: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (c. 1387–1400) in the East Midland dialect that became the basis for modern standard English, the Pearl-poet's alliterative Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (c. 1375–1400) in the North-West Midlands, William Langland's Piers Plowman, the mystical writings of Julian of Norwich, and Malory's late-fifteenth-century Le Morte d'Arthur.

alphabet.name: a
alphabet.notes: Long ā in 'name', 'tale'; short a in 'cat', 'man'. Length distinguished phonemically.

alphabet.name: be
alphabet.notes: As in modern English.

alphabet.name: ce
alphabet.notes: Following Norman scribal practice; word-initial 'c' before 'i' or 'e' is /s/ ('citee', 'cercle').

alphabet.name: de
alphabet.notes: As in modern English.

alphabet.name: e
alphabet.notes: Long ē in 'sweete' /eː/; short e in 'bed' /ɛ/; final unstressed -e is the 'reduced' vowel /ə/, often pronounced in Chaucerian scansion.

alphabet.name: ef
alphabet.notes: Voicing between vowels persists from Old English in some words.

alphabet.name: ge
alphabet.notes: Hard g in 'good', 'gilde'; soft g in 'gentil' (from French).

alphabet.name: ha
alphabet.notes: Aspirated word-initially; sometimes silent in Romance loans.

alphabet.name: i
alphabet.notes: Long ī in 'tyme' (note 'y' is just an alternative spelling for ī in many positions); short i in 'sittë'.

alphabet.name: ka
alphabet.notes: Used after Norman scribal habits where Old English used 'c' (knight, knew — k once pronounced).

alphabet.name: el
alphabet.notes: Sometimes 'dark' before consonants.

alphabet.name: em
alphabet.notes: As modern English.

alphabet.name: en
alphabet.notes: As modern English; assimilates before /k/, /ɡ/.

alphabet.name: o
alphabet.notes: Spelling -oo- usually marks the long /oː/ ('roote'); single o in 'open' is short /ɔ/.

alphabet.name: pe
alphabet.notes: Unaspirated like Romance languages, generally.

alphabet.name: qu
alphabet.notes: Always followed by 'u' ('queene', 'quod').

alphabet.name: er
alphabet.notes: Always pronounced — never silent as in modern non-rhotic English. Tap or trill.

alphabet.name: es
alphabet.notes: Voiced between vowels; voiceless initially and finally.

alphabet.name: te
alphabet.notes: As modern; unaspirated.

alphabet.name: u/v
alphabet.notes: U and v are interchangeable scribal variants — the choice is positional, not phonemic. Same letter in this period.

alphabet.name: wynn
alphabet.notes: Old English wynn (ƿ) had been replaced by 'w' (literally 'double-u').

alphabet.name: ex
alphabet.notes: Rare except in Greek loans and a few proper nouns.

alphabet.name: y
alphabet.notes: Often interchangeable with 'i' ('tyme'/'time', 'lyf'/'lif'); sometimes a consonant /j/.

alphabet.name: zed
alphabet.notes: Rare; often replaced by 's'.

alphabet.name: thorn
alphabet.notes: Survives in Chaucer's manuscripts and the Pearl-poet, gradually replaced by 'th'. Pronunciation determined by position (voiced between vowels, voiceless elsewhere).

alphabet.name: yogh
alphabet.notes: Old English /ɣ/ or /j/. By Chaucer's time partly replaced by 'gh' (knight, night) or 'y'. Common in the Pearl-poet's manuscripts.

alphabet.name: ash
alphabet.notes: Increasingly rare in Middle English; survives in some northern manuscripts and in conservative spellings.

pronunciation_notes: Final unstressed -e was usually pronounced as a schwa /ə/ in Chaucerian verse — 'sweete' is two syllables, 'wende' two syllables, 'longe' two syllables. By the time of Caxton (c. 1480) this final -e had largely been lost, which is why later printers often retained it as a silent letter only. To scan Chaucer correctly, give -e its syllable.

The 'gh' in 'knight', 'night', 'thought' was pronounced /x/ — the German 'Bach' sound — at the front (after a back vowel: thought) or /ç/ (the German 'ich' sound; after front vowels: night). It was not silent.
The 'k' in 'knight', 'knew' was fully pronounced. So was the 'l' in 'half', 'folk'.
'r' was always pronounced — including after vowels ('herte', 'feere', 'lord'). Middle English was rhotic, like modern Scottish or American English.
'wh' was a separate phoneme /ʍ/ — a voiceless 'w', as in conservative Scottish 'whales' vs. 'Wales'.

The Great Vowel Shift had not yet happened at the start of the period and was just beginning by Chaucer's time. So 'tyme' was /tiːmə/ (rhyming with modern 'team'), 'house' was /huːs/ (rhyming with 'goose'), 'name' was /naːmə/ (close to modern 'father' + uh).
Stress in native Germanic words remained on the root syllable as in Old English; stress in French loans was variable, often shifting back to root over time ('coráge' → 'courage').
Spelling was wildly inconsistent — Chaucer's own manuscripts vary; the Pearl-poet's dialect differs sharply. Modern editors usually regularize but reading a diplomatic text means accepting variation.

grammar.noun_system: Middle English collapsed Old English's four-case system. By Chaucer's time only two distinctions survive in noun morphology: a genitive singular in -es ('the kynges sone') and a plural in -es or -en ('eyen' eyes, 'oxen' oxen). The rest is signalled by word order and prepositions. Definite article 'the' (or northern 'þe') is invariable; indefinite article 'a' / 'an' alternates by following sound. Adjectives still carry a weak/strong distinction in early Middle English (an unstressed -e marks the weak form) but this is largely gone by 1400.
grammar.verb_system: Middle English distinguishes strong verbs (vowel change: rise, ros, risen / sing, sang, sungen) from weak verbs (-ed suffix: love, lovede, loved). Person and number are still marked: 1st sg. -e ('I love'), 2nd sg. -est ('thou lovest'), 3rd sg. -eth ('he loveth'), plural -en ('we loven'). The infinitive ends in -en or -e. The past participle of strong verbs takes a 'y-' or 'i-' prefix (a continuation of Old English ge-) in Chaucer: 'y-falle', 'y-clept'. Auxiliaries 'shal' and 'wol' carry both modal and future meaning. The subjunctive is alive ('if he be', 'thogh he were').
grammar.key_features: Pronouns: 'thou/thee/thy/thyn' (2nd sg.), 'ye/you/your' (2nd pl. and polite sg.). Northern dialects use 'they/them/their' from Old Norse loans, while southern dialects retain 'hi/hem/hir'. Negation is marked by 'ne' before the verb and often a second negative particle ('nat', 'noght') after — double negatives are grammatical and emphatic, not erroneous. Word order is verb-second in main clauses but not rigidly so. Question inversion is the rule: 'what seyde he?' rather than 'what did he say?' Auxiliary 'do' has not yet become obligatory in negation or questions.
grammar.reference: For grammar, Fernand Mossé, A Handbook of Middle English (Johns Hopkins, 1952; trans. James A. Walker) remains the standard. For dialects, the Linguistic Atlas of Late Mediaeval English (Angus McIntosh et al., 1986) maps the variation. Larry D. Benson's introduction to The Riverside Chaucer (3rd ed., 1987) provides a clear pronunciation and grammar primer for Chaucerian usage.

reading_list: Harley Lyrics, plus 'Sumer is icumen in' and 'Adam lay ybounden' (shortest, easiest Middle English — the bottom rung)
The Owl and the Nightingale (early Middle English debate poem)
Wycliffite Bible, selections (the easiest continuous ME entry point; lets a reader run the same passage across Wycliffe, the Vulgate, and the Greek New Testament)
Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue (the most-read Middle English text — start here)
Chaucer, The Miller's Tale and The Wife of Bath's Prologue (vivid characterization, accessible vocabulary)
Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde (Chaucer's other masterpiece, a five-book romance in rhyme royal)
Chaucer, Boece (his Middle English prose translation of Boethius — the cross-shelf pairing with the latin De Consolatione and Alfred's Old English Boethius)
Gower, Confessio Amantis
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (anonymous, c. 1375–1400 — alliterative verse from the North-West Midlands; harder dialect but unmatched poetry)
Pearl (same Pearl-poet manuscript; a dream-vision elegy of breathtaking technical perfection)
Patience and Cleanness (the other two poems in the Cotton Nero A.x manuscript alongside Gawain and Pearl; completing a single manuscript as one product unit)
Julian of Norwich, A Revelation of Love (c. 1395; clear East Anglian prose, mystical theology)
Margery Kempe, The Book of Margery Kempe (c. 1438; the first autobiography in English)
Richard Rolle and The Cloud of Unknowing (completes the mystics cluster beside Julian and Margery)
Ancrene Wisse; Layamon's Brut
Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur (c. 1469–1470; late Middle English prose, fluent and narrative-driven; Caxton's 1485 print made it canonical)
Langland, Piers Plowman (alliterative satire; harder than Chaucer but a window into late-fourteenth-century dissent)
Mandeville's Travels; the Paston Letters (everyday prose)
The York and Wakefield mystery plays (dramatic Middle English; 'The Second Shepherds' Pageant' is a frequent classroom text)
Everyman (morality play, distinct from the biblical-cycle mystery plays already listed)
The Scots makars: Henryson's Testament of Cresseid (answers Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde), Dunbar, and Barbour's Brus (Middle Scots — a distinct register not otherwise represented)
_reading_list_notes: Additions per Jae's 2026-08-22 canon review. The Wycliffite Bible added specifically to enable a cross-shelf feature: the same biblical passage rendered in Greek, Latin (Vulgate), and Middle English side by side. Everyman added as the morality-play counterpart to the existing mystery-play entry — these are distinct dramatic genres, not duplicates.

numbers.overview: Middle English numerals are mostly inherited from Old English with phonological changes. Cardinals from one through ten: oon (or 'on'), two, three, foure, fyve, six, sevene, eighte, nyne, ten. Compound forms work as in modern English: eleven, twelve, thirtene… twenty, thirty, fourty… hundred, thousand. The Old English '-tig' suffix for tens has become '-ty'. Spelling varies wildly — 'fyve', 'fife', 'fyf' all appear; modern editors often regularize, but original manuscripts will not.

cardinals.note: Zero as a concept entered English with Arabic numerals via Italian commercial mathematics; the Middle English period mostly does without it.
Also written 'on', 'one'. Long ō. The unrounded form 'an' / 'a' became the indefinite article.
The 'w' was pronounced — silent only after the Great Vowel Shift.
Also spelled 'thre'. From Old English þrēo.
Long ī ('y' is just a spelling variant). Final -e pronounced as schwa.
The 'gh' is /ç/ — the German 'ich' sound. Disyllabic.
From Old English endleofan, lit. 'one left' (over ten).
From Old English twelf, lit. 'two left' (over ten).
Doublet 'thirty' is a metathesis already common.
From OE hundred. Note 'an hundred' with article.

ordinals.note: From Old French segund / Latin secundus.
Metathesis to 'third' was already in progress.

numbers.teaching_notes: When reading Middle English verse aloud, the most important rule is to pronounce final unstressed -e as a schwa /ə/, except where it would be elided before a following vowel or 'h' + vowel. This is what makes Chaucer's iambic pentameter scan: 'And smal-e fou-les ma-ken me-lo-dy-e' has ten syllables only if the final -es and -e are sounded. The same convention holds for syllabic -es endings ('hous-es', 'cham-bres'). Numerals follow the same rule: 'sev-e-ne' is three syllables, 'eigh-te' is two, 'fif-te' is two.
